description: We are the "Gravity Victims" team. Earth's gravity keeps us firmly on our feet, but our thoughts and ideas have long since reached outer space!
summary: The Mars Field Computer is an interactive, browser-based onboard computer designed for planning a Mars expedition. Users select one of seven locations on a real mosaic of the Martian surface to receive a "passport" for that site, detailing temperature, atmospheric pressure, radiation levels, the probability of subsurface ice, and the primary hazard. Each data point is labeled—as "measured," "reference," or "estimate"—to indicate its level of reliability. A calculator determines the required oxygen, water, battery power, and food, as well as the projected radiation dose, based on the selected mission duration, crew size, and time spent on extravehicular activity (EVA). Checklists and step-by-step emergency protocols—covering scenarios such as depressurization, dust storms, or radiation spikes—help users prepare for potential dangers. The project illustrates that selecting a landing site involves balancing scientific objectives, available resources, and risks, while making NASA mission data accessible to those without specialized expertise.
details:
The project consists of four modules:

Map. A conformal map of Mars featuring seven locations based on real-world coordinates: Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Meridiani Planum, Valles Marineris, Olympus Mons, Hellas Planitia, and Utopia Planitia.

Location Profile. Includes a photograph of the site, four key metrics with a confidence rating, the primary hazard, and a five-axis complexity chart.

Expedition Generator. A model that calculates resource requirements per sol and per Martian hour (1 sol = 24 hours, 39 minutes, 35 seconds). It also displays radiation exposure—compared to a chest CT scan—and generates a checklist that is saved in your browser. The list can be copied or printed.

Emergency Reference Guide. Contains eight scenarios with step-by-step instructions, plus an "alert mode" that displays a single step in full-screen view—designed to be readable while wearing a helmet.
